title: A Soviet Spy's Secret Shame Nearly Stopped World War III
dek: In 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran volunteered to MI6 — not for money or ideology, but because he believed the West could cure his erectile dysfunction. The intelligence he handed over led the US and Britain to give the Soviets' coup plan to the Iranians.
why: Ben Macintyre tells a Cold War spy story that has never been told, with astonishing detail and tight pacing, though the information density is concentrated in the second half — the coup and its aftermath — while the setup runs a little long.
who: Listeners interested in Cold War spy history, the Iranian Revolution, and intelligence operations; readers who like Ben Macintyre's narrative style; anyone who wants to understand how intelligence inadvertently shaped the modern Middle East.
skip: The opening sponsor ad and closing promotion can be skipped; the main episode starts at 3:01.

points.h: A spy story that has never been told
points.body: Ben Macintyre's new book Redwood tells a previously undisclosed Cold War story: in 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran, Vladimir Kuzichkin, volunteered to MI6 and became a double agent codenamed "Redwood." The intelligence he provided revealed that the Soviets were planning a coup through the Iranian communist Tudeh Party to overthrow Khomeini, after which the Red Army would cross into Iran from Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, and Turkmenistan. The Pentagon's response was a nuclear strike — because conventional forces were insufficient to stop a full Soviet invasion. What makes the story so strange is that Kuzichkin's motive for defecting was intensely personal: he suffered from erectile dysfunction and believed Western medicine could cure him.

points.h: 1981 was closer to nuclear war than the Cuban Missile Crisis
points.body: Ben Macintyre points out that 1981 was one of the closest moments of nuclear confrontation in the Cold War, second only to the Cuban Missile Crisis. After the Iranian Revolution, various forces — nationalists, liberals, communists, and Islamists — were all vying for power, and Tehran became a "seething cauldron of spies." The CIA, MI6, and KGB all poured in at the same time. The Soviets had just invaded Afghanistan and were making good progress, while the US was desperate to re-establish a foothold in the Middle East. If the Soviets took Iran, they could control warm-water ports and oil fields and win the Cold War. So the Pentagon was already drawing up nuclear response plans, including using portable nuclear weapons to blow up mountain ranges to block Soviet armored columns.

points.h: The CIA was blind in Tehran; MI6 broke the rules and left a man behind
points.body: After the Iran hostage crisis, the CIA was expelled from Tehran and had no human intelligence in Iran at all, leaving it completely in the dark about a possible Soviet coup. The only agency still capable of operating was MI6, but Britain's condition for maintaining a diplomatic mission in 1981 was "no spying of any kind." Nevertheless, MI6 sent Ian McCready in under commercial cover as a commercial counselor — a huge gamble by the British government. McCready's instructions were "do nothing, recruit no one, keep a low profile" — because if he were caught, the Iranians would take the entire embassy hostage. He could only communicate with London using a WWII-era cipher machine called RockX, which was extremely cumbersome to operate and of which only two existed worldwide.

points.h: His motive for defecting was impotence, not money or ideology
points.body: Kuzichkin was a senior officer at the KGB residency in Tehran, responsible for the entire Middle East illegal spy program, and the only defector who knew how the illegal system worked. He walked into MI6 and offered to spy for the West. The intelligence world has an acronym, MICE — money, ideology, coercion, ego — but Kuzichkin fit none of them. He was partly motivated by alienation from the regime, but the root cause was that he suffered from erectile dysfunction and believed the West had a drug that could cure it. He had just married, loved his wife deeply, and could not reveal this secret to KGB colleagues or Soviet doctors. McCready did not mock or exploit him but treated him with extreme seriousness, even sending MI6 headquarters an unprecedented telex: "Help. What do I do with a spy who has erectile dysfunction?"

points.h: He photographed every KGB document in the Middle East
points.body: For nearly a year, McCready ran Kuzichkin using old-fashioned methods: dead drops, brush contacts, miniature cameras. He gave Kuzichkin a Minox miniature camera to take into the office every day and photograph every document he could get his hands on. In the end, the Redwood archive filled four truckloads. MI6 gave him the codename "Redwood" — because he was six foot four, and because they couldn't resist the pun: Red for communism, Wood for his "problem." Kuzichkin's core intelligence was that the Soviets were planning a coup through the Tudeh Party, that funding and weapons were already in place, that the Tudeh Party had a secret military underground, and that Kuzichkin himself was the coordinator between the KGB and the Tudeh Party.

points.h: The US and Britain handed the coup plan to the Iranians
points.body: After Kuzichkin fled to Britain, MI6 debated internally whether to use the intelligence. Chris Cohn, head of the operations department (later MI6 chief), argued it had to be used. He said that if they didn't, the intelligence about the Tudeh communist coup would be meaningless. So MI6 sent Redwood to Islamabad, Pakistan, under diplomatic cover, to meet with Iranian intelligence. The meeting lasted three days, Kuzichkin told everything, and MI6 handed all four truckloads of intelligence to the Iranians. This was also an attempt to establish a secret channel of communication with Iran at a time when relations with the West were at rock bottom. It was highly illegal, and if made public would have been a huge scandal — the British and American governments intervening to protect the Islamic Revolution.

points.h: Iran used the intelligence to execute eight thousand communists
points.body: After the Revolutionary Guard received the intelligence, within two months they arrested eight thousand Iranian communists, about half of whom were executed. This became a cornerstone of Iran's modern theocratic state. From that moment on, Khomeini tolerated no opposition whatsoever; everyone was purged, including those already in prison, turning into a massacre. It also reinforced two beliefs of the Islamic Revolution: first, that all opposition must be eliminated because fifth columns were everywhere; second, that no matter what happened, the British were behind it. MI6 and the CIA inadvertently consolidated the Iranian regime and created a monster — almost an exact replay of Afghanistan: money poured in to Islamic guerrillas to fight the Soviets, ultimately giving rise to al-Qaeda, ISIS, and 9/11.

points.h: History is often driven by perceptions, not facts
points.body: Ben Macintyre stresses that it is not certain whether the Soviets would actually have carried out the coup, but all the participants believed they would. McCready believed it, Kuzichkin believed it, and MI6, the CIA, the KGB, and the Tudeh Party themselves all believed it. That was enough — nuclear war can break out based on perception rather than fact, just as with the Cuban Missile Crisis. Would Khrushchev really have used those weapons? We don't know, but everyone believed he might. This story has never been told because all the participants did not want it told: the Iranians didn't, because it would mean the West had outsmarted them again; the KGB didn't, because it was a humiliation — they failed to detect the defector, 18 Soviet diplomats were expelled from Iran as a result, the entire Tudeh Party operation was dismantled, and agent networks across the Middle East and even in Canada were exposed.
